subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: In this unit you will organise information. You will sort objects by one rule, see how the rule decides which group something belongs to, sort things into and out of a sorting circle, use a sorting box, and then read and make a pictogram and a block graph.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Mathematics 0096 — Stage 1 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: Sort a set of objects into groups using one rule, such as colour, size, shape or type.
Understand that the sorting rule (criteria) decides which group each thing goes in.
Sort things into and out of a circle (a simple Venn diagram) — ‘belongs’ or ‘does not belong’.
Sort things into a four-box Carroll diagram using a yes/no rule, with each thing in exactly one box.
Read a simple pictogram where one picture means one thing.
Make a simple pictogram or block graph by drawing one picture or block for each object.
Count the pictures in each row or column to find how many are in each group.
Compare groups using the words more, fewer/less, most and least/fewest.
Answer simple questions about a chart, such as ‘Which has the most?’ and ‘How many more?’.
Find all the possible combinations for a small set of items (two or three), such as the different orders three coloured beads can be threaded, by trying them in an organised way.

concepts.title: Sorting by One Attribute
concepts.explanation: Everything in this unit begins with sorting: putting things that are alike into the same group. The most important idea is that we sort using a rule — colour, size, shape, or type — and the rule decides where each thing belongs. You sort naturally when they tidy toys, so start there and simply give the activity its name. How to teach it: Tip out a basket of stones, dates and buttons onto the mat. Say, ‘Let us sort these. Our rule is colour.’ Make a small pile for each colour and place a few objects together, then continue. When the piles are done, count each one aloud: ‘Three brown, five white, two black.’ Then do the same objects again with a new rule — ‘Now let us sort by size: big things here, small things there.’ Seeing the *same* objects fall into *different* groups when the rule changes is the heart of sorting. 🗣 Suggested dialogue You: “Look at all these stones. Let us put them into groups. Our rule is colour.” You: “Where does this white stone go?” Child: “With the white ones!” You: “Well done. Now count this group with me. One, two, three. Three white stones.” You: “Let us try a new rule — big and small. Watch how the groups change!”
concepts.example: Talk about why each thing goes where it goes: ‘This one is white, so it belongs with the white group.’ Naming the reason helps you hold the rule in mind. Keep the first rules very clear and obvious — colour is the easiest — before trying trickier rules such as ‘things that roll’ or ‘things made of metal’. Always finish by counting each group, because counting is what turns a pile into data we can compare.

concepts.title: The Sorting Circle (Venn Diagram)
concepts.explanation: A Venn diagram is just a circle with a rule. Things that fit the rule go inside the circle; things that do not stay outside. For Year 1 we use only one circle — overlapping circles come much later. Make the circle real: a loop of string or a scarf on the floor is far better than a drawing at this age. How to teach it: Lay a string loop on the mat and say, ‘Inside this circle we put red things. Everything else stays outside.’ Hand the child objects one at a time — a red button, a green date, a red bead — and ask, ‘Does this belong inside or outside?’ Let them place each one. You are learning that every object either belongs to the group or does not belong, with nothing in between. 🗣 Suggested dialogue You: “Inside the circle goes everything that is red. Ready?” You: “Here is a red button. Inside or outside?” Child: “Inside!” You: “Here is a green leaf. Inside or outside?” Child: “Outside — it is not red.” You: “Yes! Only red things belong inside our circle.”
concepts.example: Once the objects are placed, count what is inside and what is outside, and say it out loud: ‘Four red things are inside. Six things are outside.’ Try different rules on other days — ‘animals with four legs’, ‘things that are round’, ‘fruit’ — so you see the circle can hold any group we choose, as long as we agree on the rule first.

concepts.title: The Sorting Box (Carroll Diagram)
concepts.explanation: A Carroll diagram is a box divided into sections that sorts by a yes/no rule. The simplest version has just two boxes — for example ‘furry’ and ‘not furry’ — and every object must go in exactly one box. This is a gentle first step and is plenty for many Year 1 children; a full Carroll diagram with four boxes uses two rules at once and can be offered to confident children as an extension. How to teach it: Fold a sheet of paper in two and label the halves ‘furry’ and ‘not furry’ (draw a little picture as a reminder, since you cannot read the words). Give the child toy animals or picture cards and ask, ‘Is a goat furry? Then it goes in the furry box.’ The key habit to build is that each thing goes in one box only — if it is furry it cannot also be in the ‘not furry’ box. Keep asking ‘why did you put it there?’ to check your thinking. 🗣 Suggested dialogue You: “This side is for furry animals. This side is for not-furry animals.” You: “Is a camel furry?” Child: “Yes!” You: “So which box?” Child: “The furry box.” You: “Is a fish furry?” Child: “No.” You: “Good — it goes in the not-furry box, only there.”
concepts.example: Yes/no rules that work well include big/small, red/not red, and rolls/does not roll. Because a Carroll diagram forces a clear ‘yes or no’ choice, it is a wonderful way to talk about how we make decisions when sorting. When the boxes are full, count each one so the sorting again becomes data to compare.

concepts.title: Reading a Pictogram
concepts.explanation: A pictogram shows data using pictures in neat rows, where one picture means one thing. Because the rows line up, you can see at a glance which group is biggest without even counting — the longest row is the most. Start by *reading* ready-made pictograms before asking you to make one. How to teach it: Show the ‘Favourite fruit’ pictogram idea — a row of five mangoes, a row of three bananas, a row of two oranges — and make sure it has a title so we know what it shows. Point to each row and count: ‘Mangoes — one, two, three, four, five. Five people chose mango.’ Then ask the comparing questions: ‘Which row is longest? Which fruit is the most? Which is the least? How many more chose mango than orange?’ 🗣 Suggested dialogue You: “This chart shows favourite fruit. Each picture means one person.” You: “Let us count the mango row. One, two, three, four, five.” You: “Which row is the longest?” Child: “Mango!” You: “So mango is the most popular.” You: “How many more people chose mango than orange? Let us match them and see.”
concepts.example: Two habits matter most here. First, keep the pictures the same size and lined up with no gaps, or the rows lie about which is longer. Second, always look for the title — without it, a chart is a mystery. Remember that a pictogram is really just the sorting groups from before, stood up in rows so we can compare them easily.

concepts.title: Making a Pictogram or Block Graph
concepts.explanation:
A block graph is the pictogram's simple cousin: instead of a picture, we colour one block for each thing. Blocks are quicker to draw than pictures, so block graphs are a lovely way for a small child to make their own chart. The rule is the same — one block per object, no gaps, all starting from the same line.

How to teach it: Run a tiny survey first. Ask three or four family members, ‘What is your favourite animal — goat, camel or chicken?’ Record each answer with a tally mark or a sticky note. Then build the chart together: colour one block for each vote, keeping the columns neat and side by side. Give it a title and simple labels (a little drawing of each animal). Finally, read it back: ‘Camel has the most blocks. Chicken has the fewest.’
concepts.example: Keep your very first charts small — three groups of a few objects each is perfect. The point is not a beautiful chart but the understanding that each block or picture stands for one real thing, and that a taller column means more. Making a chart from data they collected themselves is deeply satisfying and cements the whole unit.

concepts.title: Comparing Groups — More, Fewer, Most, Least
concepts.explanation: The reason we sort and chart at all is to compare. This concept threads through every other one. Give the child the four comparing words and use them constantly: more, fewer (or less), most, least (or fewest). ‘Most’ is the biggest group of all; ‘least’ is the smallest. How to teach it: Put two groups side by side — say 6 dates and 4 dates — and ask, ‘Which has more? Which has fewer?’ The most reliable check for a young child is matching one-to-one: pair a date from each group; whichever group has dates left over has more. To find ‘how many more’, count the leftovers. For three or more groups, line them up as rows and the longest is the most, the shortest is the least. 🗣 Suggested dialogue You: “Here are the dogs and the fish from our chart. Which row is longer?” Child: “The dogs.” You: “So there are more dogs. Dogs are the most.” You: “How many more dogs than fish? Let us match them in pairs and count what is left over.” Practise the words in real life all week — more sandals by the door than yesterday, fewer dates on the plate after iftar, the most cups on the mat. When the comparing words become part of ordinary talk, reading charts becomes easy, because a chart is just a neat way to see ‘which has more’ at a glance. Putting one thing in two groups. In a Carroll or circle sort, each object belongs in exactly one place. Keep rules clear and mutually exclusive at first (red / not red), and ask ‘why does it go there?’. Thinking a spread-out or big-object group ‘looks like more’. A row of large stones can look longer than a row of more small buttons. Use one-to-one matching to compare, not just a glance.
concepts.example: Leaving gaps in a pictogram or block graph. Gaps make a short row look long. Model starting every row from the same line with no spaces between pictures.

concepts.title: Finding All the Combinations
concepts.explanation: Some problems ask not for a single answer but for every possible way something could happen — this is called finding combinations. Working through them one at a time, in an organised order, stops you from missing one or repeating one by accident. How to teach it: Give the child three differently coloured beads, such as red, blue and yellow, and a piece of string. Ask, 'In how many different orders can you thread these three beads?' Fix one bead first (say, red first) and then try both orders of the remaining two beads, before moving on to a different bead first. Write or draw each order found, such as red-blue-yellow, red-yellow-blue, and so on, checking off each one. This same idea works for other small combination questions, such as, 'You have a red shirt and a blue shirt, and yellow shorts and green shorts — how many different outfits can you make?' (four: pairing each shirt with each pair of shorts). Keep the total number of items small (two or three) so you can find every combination by careful, organised trying rather than by guessing.
concepts.example: 🗣 Suggested dialogue You: “You have a red bead, a blue bead and a yellow bead. How many different orders can you thread them onto the string?” Child: tries red-blue-yellow. You: “Good, write that down. Now try starting with red again, but swap the last two.” Child: tries red-yellow-blue. You: “Now let's start with blue instead...” Continue until you find all six orders, checking each one off a list so none is repeated or missed.

explorations.title: Sorting by One Attribute
explorations.context: Everything in this unit begins with sorting: putting things that are alike into the same group. The most important idea is that we sort using a rule — colour, size, shape, or type — and the rule decides where each thing belongs.
explorations.prompt: If you sort stones by colour and pick up a white stone, which group does it join?
explorations.hint: Look at the stone's colour, then find the pile with that same colour.
explorations.explanation: Sorting only works once everyone agrees on the rule — colour, size, shape or type — because the very same objects fall into different groups depending on which rule is chosen. Have you name the rule out loud before they start, then count each finished group together.

explorations.title: The Sorting Circle (Venn Diagram)
explorations.context: A Venn diagram is just a circle with a rule. Things that fit the rule go inside the circle; things that do not stay outside. For Year 1 we use only one circle — overlapping circles come much later.
explorations.prompt: A circle's rule is 'red things'. A green leaf is placed next to it. Does the leaf go inside or outside the circle?
explorations.hint: Check if the leaf matches the circle's rule — is it red?
explorations.explanation: A single circle tests one rule at a time: anything that matches goes inside, and anything that does not stays outside, with no in-between. Making the circle real with a loop of string lets you physically place each object and see the decision, rather than just imagining it.

explorations.title: The Sorting Box (Carroll Diagram)
explorations.context: A Carroll diagram is a box divided into sections that sorts by a yes/no rule. The simplest version has just two boxes — for example ‘furry’ and ‘not furry’ — and every object must go in exactly one box.
explorations.prompt: A sorting box has 'furry' and 'not furry' sides. Which side does a fish go in?
explorations.hint: Ask yourself: does a fish have fur?
explorations.explanation: A sorting box uses a yes/no question to split everything into exactly two groups, so every object has one true home — never both sides, never neither. Asking the question aloud for each item, such as 'Is it furry?', keeps you focused on the rule rather than guessing.

explorations.title: Reading a Pictogram
explorations.context: A pictogram shows data using pictures in neat rows, where one picture means one thing. Because the rows line up, you can see at a glance which group is biggest without even counting — the longest row is the most.
explorations.prompt: A pictogram shows 5 mango pictures and 3 banana pictures. Which row is the longest?
explorations.hint: Compare how many pictures are in each row — the longest row has the most.
explorations.explanation: Because every row lines up picture by picture, the longest row is the biggest group and can be spotted at a glance without even counting — counting each row just confirms it. Always check the title first, since that is what tells you what the pictures actually represent.

explorations.title: Making a Pictogram or Block Graph
explorations.context: A block graph is the pictogram's simple cousin: instead of a picture, we colour one block for each thing. Blocks are quicker to draw than pictures, so block graphs are a lovely way for a small child to make their own chart.
explorations.prompt: Three friends choose their favourite animal: goat, chick, goat. How many blocks should you colour in the goat row?
explorations.hint: Count only the friends who said goat.
explorations.explanation: Drawing a chart from scratch teaches the same rule as reading one: one block or picture for every single answer, lined up from the same starting point with no gaps. Running a tiny real survey first, then drawing the results together, makes it obvious why the chart has to work this way.

explorations.title: Comparing Groups — More, Fewer, Most, Least
explorations.context: The reason we sort and chart at all is to compare. This concept threads through every other one. Give the child the four comparing words and use them constantly: more, fewer (or less), most, least (or fewest).
explorations.prompt: Goat: 🐐🐐🐐🐐🐐 (5). Chick: 🐤🐤 (2). Which animal has more?
explorations.hint: Match one goat to one chick — whichever has some left over has more.
explorations.explanation: Once data is sorted or charted, the whole point is comparing it — most is the biggest group, least is the smallest, and more/fewer describe any two groups side by side. Matching items one-to-one between two groups is the most reliable way for a young child to check which group truly has more.

methods.title: Sort Objects Using One Rule
methods.example: Sort a bowl of dates, buttons and stones by colour.
steps: Choose one rule to sort by, such as colour, size or shape.
Look at each object and decide which group it matches.
Put the object in that group, then count how many are in each group when you finish.

methods.title: Sort Things Into a Circle
methods.example: Lay a string loop on the mat as the 'red things' circle.
steps: Decide the circle's rule, for example 'red things'.
Pick up each object and ask, does it match the rule?
Place it inside the circle if it matches, or outside if it does not.

methods.title: Sort Things Into a Sorting Box
methods.example: Fold paper in two and label the sides 'furry' and 'not furry'.
steps: Label the two sides of the box with a yes/no rule, such as 'furry' and 'not furry'.
Ask the yes/no question for each object, such as 'Is it furry?'
Place every object in exactly one side, never both.

methods.title: Read a Pictogram
methods.example: A fruit pictogram shows 5 mangoes, 3 bananas and 2 oranges.
steps: Check the title to see what the pictogram shows.
Count the pictures in one row to find how many that group has.
Compare the rows to see which is longest and which is shortest.

methods.title: Make a Pictogram of Favourite Animals
methods.example: Ask family members to choose goat, camel or chick, then draw one picture for each answer.
steps: Ask each person to choose one favourite animal: goat, camel or chick.
Draw one picture in the correct row for every answer, with no gaps.
Add a title so anyone can tell what the pictogram shows.

methods.title: Compare Rows Using More, Fewer, Most, Least
methods.example: The goat row has 5 pictures; the chick row has 2 pictures.
steps: Count the pictures in each row you want to compare.
Match one picture from each row to a partner, one for one.
Whichever row has pictures left over is more; the other is fewer.

workedExamples.title: Sort Objects Using One Rule
workedExamples.prompt: Sort these stones by colour: 3 white stones, 2 black stones and 1 brown stone. Put each stone into its colour group.
workedExamples.solution: Look at each stone's colour. Put the 3 white stones together, the 2 black stones together, and the 1 brown stone on its own. Now there are three groups: white (3), black (2), brown (1) — one group for each colour.

workedExamples.title: Sort Things Into a Circle
workedExamples.prompt: A circle on the mat is the 'fruit' circle. You are given a mango, a button and a banana. Which things go inside the circle?
workedExamples.solution: Check each object against the rule 'fruit'. A mango is a fruit, so it goes inside. A banana is a fruit, so it goes inside. A button is not a fruit, so it stays outside. The circle ends up with 2 things inside (mango, banana) and 1 outside (button).

workedExamples.title: Sort Things Into a Sorting Box
workedExamples.prompt: A sorting box has two sides: 'furry' and 'not furry'. Sort a camel, a fish and a goat.
workedExamples.solution: Ask 'is it furry?' for each animal. A camel is furry, so it goes in the 'furry' side. A goat is furry, so it also goes in the 'furry' side. A fish is not furry, so it goes in the 'not furry' side. Every animal is in exactly one side.

workedExamples.title: Read a Pictogram
workedExamples.prompt: A pictogram shows favourite fruit: 5 mango pictures, 3 banana pictures, 2 orange pictures. How many children chose orange?
workedExamples.solution: The title tells us this is about favourite fruit. Find the orange row and count its pictures: 1, 2. There are 2 pictures in the orange row, so 2 children chose orange.

workedExamples.title: Make a Pictogram of Favourite Animals
workedExamples.prompt: Three friends choose their favourite animal: goat, chick, goat. Draw a pictogram to show this.
workedExamples.solution: Two friends said goat, so draw 2 pictures in the goat row. One friend said chick, so draw 1 picture in the chick row. Give the chart a title, 'Favourite Animal', so everyone knows what it shows.

workedExamples.title: Compare Rows Using More, Fewer, Most, Least
workedExamples.prompt: Goat: 🐐🐐🐐🐐🐐 (5). Chick: 🐤🐤 (2). Which animal has more votes?
workedExamples.solution: Count each row: goat has 5 pictures, chick has 2 pictures. Match them one to one — goat has 3 pictures left over after pairing with chick. Since 5 is bigger than 2, goat has more votes.

workedExamples.title: Count the Camel Row
workedExamples.prompt: Camel: 🐫🐫🐫. How many children chose camel?
workedExamples.solution: Count the camel pictures one at a time: 1, 2, 3. There are 3 pictures, so 3 children chose camel.

workedExamples.title: Count the Chick Row
workedExamples.prompt: Chick: 🐤🐤. How many children chose chick?
workedExamples.solution: Count the chick pictures one at a time: 1, 2. There are 2 pictures, so 2 children chose chick.

workedExamples.title: Which Animal Has the Most?
workedExamples.prompt: Goat: 5 pictures. Camel: 3 pictures. Chick: 2 pictures. Which animal has the most votes?
workedExamples.solution: Compare all three rows: 5, 3 and 2. The biggest number is 5, and that is the goat row. So goat has the most votes.

workedExamples.title: Which Animal Has the Least?
workedExamples.prompt: Goat: 5 pictures. Camel: 3 pictures. Chick: 2 pictures. Which animal has the least votes?
workedExamples.solution: Compare all three rows: 5, 3 and 2. The smallest number is 2, and that is the chick row. So chick has the least votes.

workedExamples.title: How Many More Chose Goat Than Chick?
workedExamples.prompt: Goat: 5 pictures. Chick: 2 pictures. How many more children chose goat than chick?
workedExamples.solution: Start with the goat count, 5. Take away the chick count, 2: 5 − 2 = 3. So 3 more children chose goat than chick.

workedExamples.title: Sort Into the Circle
workedExamples.prompt: A circle is the 'four legs' circle. Sort a goat, a chick and a camel.
workedExamples.solution: Ask 'does it have four legs?' for each animal. A goat has four legs, so it goes inside the circle. A camel has four legs, so it also goes inside. A chick has two legs, so it stays outside the circle.

practice.prompt: Sort these stones by colour: 3 white, 2 black, 1 brown. How many groups do you make?
practice.hint: Count how many different colours there are.

practice.prompt: A circle is the 'fruit' circle. A mango, a button and a banana are given. How many things go inside the circle?
practice.hint: Ask which of the three things are fruit.

practice.prompt: A sorting box has 'furry' and 'not furry' sides. Sort a camel, a fish and a goat. Which side has the most animals?
practice.answer: The 'furry' side, with 2 animals (camel and goat).
practice.hint: Decide furry or not furry for each animal first.

practice.prompt: A pictogram shows 5 mango pictures, 3 banana pictures and 2 orange pictures. How many children chose banana?
practice.hint: Count the pictures in the banana row only.

practice.prompt: Three friends choose goat, chick, goat as their favourite animal. How many pictures should be in the goat row?
practice.hint: Count how many friends said goat.

practice.prompt: Goat: 🐐🐐🐐🐐🐐. How many goat pictures are there?
practice.hint: Count each goat picture one at a time.

practice.prompt: Camel: 🐫🐫🐫. How many camel pictures are there?
practice.hint: Count each camel picture one at a time.

practice.prompt: Chick: 🐤🐤. How many chick pictures are there?
practice.hint: Count each chick picture one at a time.

practice.prompt: Goat: 5. Camel: 3. Chick: 2. Which animal has the MOST votes?
practice.hint: Find the biggest number of pictures.

practice.prompt: Goat: 5. Camel: 3. Chick: 2. Which animal has the LEAST votes?
practice.hint: Find the smallest number of pictures.

practice.prompt: Goat: 5. Chick: 2. How many more children chose goat than chick?
practice.hint: Subtract the chick count from the goat count.

practice.prompt: A circle is the 'four legs' circle. Sort a goat, a chick and a camel. How many animals go inside?
practice.hint: Check which animals have four legs.

activities.title: Practise together
activities.materials: Paper, pencil and familiar household objects
steps: Choose one idea from this unit.
Build or draw a model of it.
Explain your model to a family member.
Write one question of your own and solve it.

rules.title: Sorting Objects Using One Rule
rules.text: Sort a set of objects into groups using one rule, such as colour, size, shape or type.

rules.title: The Sorting Rule Decides the Group
rules.text: Understand that the sorting rule (criteria) decides which group each thing goes in.

rules.title: The Four-Box Carroll Diagram
rules.text: Sort things into a four-box Carroll diagram using a yes/no rule, with each thing in exactly one box.

rules.title: Choosing Objects With Obvious Differences
rules.text: Objects that vary in an obvious way — different colours, sizes or shapes — so a sorting rule is easy to see.

rules.title: Sorting by One Attribute
rules.text: Everything in this unit begins with sorting: putting things that are alike into the same group. The most important idea is that we sort using a rule — colour, size, shape, or type — and the rule decides where each thing belongs. You sort naturally when they tidy toys, so start there and simply give the activity its name.

rules.title: How to teach it: tip and sort
rules.text: How to teach it: Tip out a basket of stones, dates and buttons onto the mat. Say, ‘Let us sort these. Our rule is colour.’ Make a small pile for each colour and place a few objects together, then continue. When the piles are done, count each one aloud: ‘Three brown, five white, two black.’ Then do the same objects again with a new rule — ‘Now let us sort by size: big things here, small things there.’ Seeing the *same* objects fall into *different* groups when the rule changes is the heart of sorting.

terms: The idea we use to sort
A set of things that are alike in one way
A chart that uses pictures to show data
A chart that uses one block for each thing
The name that tells what a chart shows
commonMistakes: A common mistake is including the chick because it is an animal. A chick has two legs, not four, so it stays outside
Only the goat and camel go inside.

fluency.prompt: Sort by colour: 4 red beads, 2 blue beads. How many groups?
fluency.hint: Look at how many different colours there are.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is counting the total beads (6) instead of the number of colour groups. There are 6 beads in total, but only 2 groups because there are only 2 colours.

fluency.prompt: A circle is the 'round things' circle. A ball, a book and a coin are given. How many things go inside?
fluency.hint: Ask which objects are round in shape.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is putting the book inside because it is an object, not because it is round. A book is not round, so it stays outside the circle.

fluency.prompt: A sorting box has 'has wheels' and 'no wheels' sides. Sort a bicycle, a spoon and a car. Which side has more?
fluency.answer: The 'has wheels' side, with 2 objects (bicycle and car).
fluency.hint: Check each object for wheels before deciding.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is putting the spoon in the 'has wheels' side by accident. A spoon has no wheels, so it belongs in the 'no wheels' side.

fluency.prompt: A pictogram shows 5 mango, 3 banana, 2 orange pictures. Which row is the longest?
fluency.hint: Compare the length of each row, not just one number.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is picking the orange row because it is listed last. The mango row has the most pictures (5), so it is the longest.

fluency.prompt: Three friends choose goat, chick, goat. If you draw one block per answer, how many blocks are in the chick row?
fluency.hint: Count only the friends who chose chick.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is drawing 2 blocks for chick by confusing it with the goat row. Only one friend chose chick, so the chick row needs just 1 block.

fluency.hint: Touch each picture once as you count.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is counting a picture twice and getting 6. Counting each of the 5 pictures exactly once gives 5.

fluency.hint: Touch each picture once as you count.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is skipping the last picture and stopping at 2. Counting all three pictures gives 3.

fluency.hint: Touch each picture once as you count.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is saying 1 because the pictures are close together. There are 2 separate chick pictures, so the count is 2.

fluency.prompt: Goat: 5. Camel: 3. Chick: 2. Which animal has the MOST votes?
fluency.hint: The row with the biggest number is the most.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is choosing camel because it is in the middle of the list. Goat has the biggest number, 5, so goat has the most votes.

fluency.prompt: Goat: 5. Camel: 3. Chick: 2. Which animal has the LEAST votes?
fluency.hint: The row with the smallest number is the least.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is choosing camel because it is not the goat. Chick has the smallest number, 2, so chick has the least votes.

fluency.prompt: Goat: 5. Chick: 2. How many more children chose goat than chick?
fluency.hint: Subtract the smaller count from the bigger count.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is adding 5 + 2 = 7 instead of subtracting. The correct working is 5 − 2 = 3, so 3 more children chose goat.

fluency.prompt: A circle is the 'four legs' circle. Sort a goat, a chick and a camel. How many go inside the circle?
fluency.hint: Check how many legs each animal has.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is including the chick because it is an animal. A chick has two legs, not four, so it stays outside — only the goat and camel go inside.

realProblems.prompt: At home, you sort the fruit bowl: 4 mangoes, 1 banana, 2 oranges. Which fruit has the least?
realProblems.hint: Find the smallest group in the fruit bowl.
realProblems.errorFeedback: A common mistake is choosing orange because it seems like a small fruit; but 'least' means the smallest count. Banana has only 1, which is fewer than orange's 2.

realProblems.prompt: At the market, a stall sold 5 goats and 2 chickens last week. How many more goats were sold than chickens?
realProblems.hint: Subtract the smaller number from the bigger number.
realProblems.errorFeedback: A common mistake is subtracting the wrong way round (2 − 5). Since we compare goats to chickens, the working is 5 − 2 = 3.

realProblems.prompt: While travelling, you see a circle drawn as the 'things that fly' group. A bird, a car and a plane pass by. Which things go inside the circle?
realProblems.answer: The bird and the plane (2 things).
realProblems.errorFeedback: A common mistake is including the car because it moves fast. A car does not fly, so only the bird and plane belong inside the circle.

realProblems.prompt: Every morning you sort your toys by colour: 3 red toys, 5 blue toys, 1 green toy. Which colour group has the least?
realProblems.errorFeedback: A common mistake is choosing red because it has fewer toys than blue; but green has only 1 toy, which is the true least.

realProblems.prompt: At snack time, 6 children chose dates and 4 children chose bananas. How many more children chose dates than bananas?
realProblems.hint: Subtract the banana count from the date count.
realProblems.errorFeedback: A common mistake is adding all 10 children together instead of finding the difference. The correct working is 6 − 4 = 2.

realProblems.prompt: You draw a circle for 'soft things'. A stone, a cushion and a cotton scarf are on the mat. Which things go inside the circle?
realProblems.answer: The cushion and the scarf (2 things).
realProblems.hint: Ask which objects feel soft to touch.
realProblems.errorFeedback: A common mistake is including the stone because it is small and light. A stone is hard, not soft, so it stays outside the circle.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: You see a row of pictures: Camel: 🐫🐫🐫. Explain how you would count them and what the count tells you.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: I would touch each camel picture and count one at a time: 1, 2, 3. This tells me that 3 children chose camel, because in a pictogram each picture is data that stands for one real answer, and counting the row tells us how many are in that group.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: You see a row of pictures: Chick: 🐤🐤. Explain how you would count them and what group they belong to.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: I would count each chick picture one at a time: 1, 2. This tells me the chick group has 2 pictures. Sorting the pictures by animal into rows like this lets me see how many children are in the chick group compared to the other groups.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: In the favourite animal pictogram, goat has 5 pictures, camel has 3 and chick has 2. Explain which animal has the most and how you know.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Goat has the most because its row has 5 pictures, and 5 is bigger than camel's 3 and chick's 2. In a pictogram, the longest row — the one with the most pictures — always shows the group with the most.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Reading a Pictogram.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A pictogram shows data using pictures in neat rows, where one picture means one thing. Because the rows line up, you can see at a glance which group is biggest without even counting — the longest row is the most. Start by *reading* ready-made pictograms before asking you to make one. How to teach it: Show the ‘Favourite fruit’ pictogram idea — a row of five mangoes, a row of three bananas, a row of two oranges — and make sure it has a title so we know what it shows. Point to each row and count: ‘Mangoes — one, two, three, four, five. Five people chose mango.’ Then ask the comparing questions: ‘Which row is longest? Which fruit is the most? Which is the least? How many more chose mango than orange?’

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Making a Pictogram or Block Graph.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer:
A block graph is the pictogram's simple cousin: instead of a picture, we colour one block for each thing. Blocks are quicker to draw than pictures, so block graphs are a lovely way for a small child to make their own chart. The rule is the same — one block per object, no gaps, all starting from the same line.

How to teach it: Run a tiny survey first. Ask three or four family members, ‘What is your favourite animal — goat, camel or chicken?’ Record each answer with a tally mark or a sticky note. Then build the chart together: colour one block for each vote, keeping the columns neat and side by side. Give it a title and simple labels (a little drawing of each animal). Finally, read it back: ‘Camel has the most blocks. Chicken has the fewest.’

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Comparing Groups — More, Fewer, Most, Least.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The reason we sort and chart at all is to compare. This concept threads through every other one. Give the child the four comparing words and use them constantly: more, fewer (or less), most, least (or fewest). ‘Most’ is the biggest group of all; ‘least’ is the smallest. How to teach it: Put two groups side by side — say 6 dates and 4 dates — and ask, ‘Which has more? Which has fewer?’ The most reliable check for a young child is matching one-to-one: pair a date from each group; whichever group has dates left over has more. To find ‘how many more’, count the leftovers. For three or more groups, line them up as rows and the longest is the most, the shortest is the least.

selfAssessment: I can sort a set of objects into groups using one rule, such as colour, size, shape or type.
I can understand that the sorting rule (criteria) decides which group each thing goes in.
I can sort things into and out of a circle (a simple Venn diagram) — ‘belongs’ or ‘does not belong’.
I can sort things into a four-box Carroll diagram using a yes/no rule, with each thing in exactly one box.
I can read a simple pictogram where one picture means one thing.
I can make a simple pictogram or block graph by drawing one picture or block for each object.
I can count the pictures in each row or column to find how many are in each group.
I can compare groups using the words more, fewer/less, most and least/fewest.
